source_refs.note: Book p. 91-92: 6.2.1 choosing 3, 4 and last four terms, A.P. kept under +, -, x, / by the same number and term-by-term sums; Examples 2-5. Teaching notes, Key points, Common mistakes are ours.

items: (i) Three consecutive terms of an A.P. can be chosen as \(a - d, a, a + d\) or \(a, a + d, a + 2d\).
(ii) Four consecutive terms of an A.P. may be written as \(a - 3d, a - d, a + d, a + 3d\) or \(a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d\).
(iii) The last four consecutive terms, if \(\ell\) is the last term, can be written as \(\ell - 3d, \ell - 2d, \ell - d, \ell\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why choose terms symmetrically? When the sum of the terms is given, the \(d\)'s cancel:
\[(a - d) + a + (a + d) = 3a\]
\[(a - 3d) + (a - d) + (a + d) + (a + 3d) = 4a\]
So one equation gives \(a\) at once, and the second condition gives \(d\).
Careful: in \(a - 3d, a - d, a + d, a + 3d\) consecutive terms differ by \(2d\), so the common difference of this A.P. is \(2d\), not \(d\).
Choose \(\ell - 3d, \ell - 2d, \ell - d, \ell\) when the question gives information about the last term.

If each term of an A.P. is increased or decreased, multiplied or divided by the same non-zero number, then the resulting sequence is also an A.P., i.e., if \(a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots, a_{n}, \ldots\) are in A.P., then

items: (i) \(a_{1} \pm k, a_{2} \pm k, \ldots, a_{n} \pm k, \ldots\) are also in A.P. with common difference \(d\).
(ii) \(ka_{1}, ka_{2}, \ldots, ka_{n}, \ldots\) are in A.P. with common difference \(kd\).
(iii) \(\frac{a_{1}}{k}, \frac{a_{2}}{k}, \ldots, \frac{a_{n}}{k}, \ldots\) are in A.P. with common difference \(\frac{d}{k}\).

(iv) Term-by-term addition or subtraction of two arithmetic progressions is also an A.P., i.e., if \(a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots, a_{n}, \ldots\) and \(b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}, \ldots, b_{n}, \ldots\) are in A.P., then \(a_{1} \pm b_{1}, a_{2} \pm b_{2}, a_{3} \pm b_{3}, \ldots\) are also in A.P.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why these are true, using \(a_{n} - a_{n-1} = d\):
(i) \((a_{n} + k) - (a_{n-1} + k) = a_{n} - a_{n-1} = d\): adding the same \(k\) shifts every term, the gaps stay \(d\).
(ii) \(ka_{n} - ka_{n-1} = k(a_{n} - a_{n-1}) = kd\).
(iii) \(\frac{a_{n}}{k} - \frac{a_{n-1}}{k} = \frac{d}{k}\); here \(k \ne 0\) because we cannot divide by zero.
(iv) If the two A.P.s have common differences \(d_{1}\) and \(d_{2}\), the new one has common difference \(d_{1} \pm d_{2}\).
Example: \(1, 3, 5, \ldots\) doubled is \(2, 6, 10, \ldots\) with \(d = 4 = 2 \times 2\).
The book's sentence for (iii) is printed in broken form ("... A.P are in A.P. common difference"); its meaning is as written above.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.problem: Find the general term and the eleventh term of the A.P. whose first term and common difference are 2 and \(-3\) respectively. Also write its first four terms.
steps:
Given: \(a_{1} = 2\), \(d = -3\).
To find: the general term \(a_{n}\), the eleventh term \(a_{11}\), and the first four terms.
Method: put \(a_{1}\) and \(d\) into \(a_{n} = a_{1} + (n-1)d\) to get a rule in \(n\), then substitute values of \(n\).

Step 1: General term
\[a_{n} = a_{1} + (n-1)d\]
\[a_{n} = 2 + (n-1)(-3)\]
\[= 2 - 3n + 3\]
\[a_{n} = 5 - 3n \quad \text{...(i)}\]
Why: \((n - 1)(-3) = -3n + 3\); a minus times a minus gives plus 3.

Step 2: Eleventh term, put \(n = 11\) in (i)
\[a_{11} = 5 - 3(11)\]
\[= 5 - 33 = -28\]
Why: once the general term is known, any term comes from its position directly.

Check:
\(a_{1}\) from (i): \(5 - 3 = 2\). Correct.
The terms \(2, -1, -4, -7\) decrease by 3 each time, as \(d = -3\) requires.
\(a_{11} = a_{1} + 10d = 2 - 30 = -28\). Correct.

blocks.title: Example 3
blocks.problem: If the 5th term of an A.P. is 13 and the 17th term is 49, find \(a_{n}\) and \(a_{13}\).
steps:
Given: \(a_{5} = 13\) and \(a_{17} = 49\).
To find: \(a_{n}\) and \(a_{13}\).
Method: write both given terms with \(a_{n} = a_{1} + (n-1)d\); this gives two equations in the two unknowns \(a_{1}\) and \(d\).

Step 1: Equation from the 5th term
\[a_{5} = a_{1} + (5-1)d\]
\[13 = a_{1} + 4d \quad \text{...(i)}\]
Why: putting \(n = 5\) in the general term.

Step 2: Equation from the 17th term
\[a_{17} = a_{1} + (17-1)d\]
\[49 = a_{1} + 16d\]
\[49 = (a_{1} + 4d) + 12d\]
\[49 = 13 + 12d \quad \text{by (i)}\]
Why: the book splits \(16d\) as \(4d + 12d\) so that \(a_{1} + 4d\), which is 13 by (i), appears.

Step 4: Find \(a_{13}\) and \(a_{n}\)
\[a_{13} = 1 + (13-1)3 = 37\]
\[a_{n} = 1 + (n-1)3 = 3n - 2\]
Why: with \(a_{1} = 1\), \(d = 3\) the general term is complete.

Check:
\(a_{5} = 3(5) - 2 = 13\) and \(a_{17} = 3(17) - 2 = 49\). Both given terms are reproduced.

blocks.title: Example 4
blocks.problem: Find the number of terms in the A.P. if \(a_{1} = 3\), \(d = 7\) and \(a_{n} = 59\).
steps:
Given: \(a_{1} = 3\), \(d = 7\), \(a_{n} = 59\) (the last term).
To find: \(n\), the number of terms.
Method: the last term is the \(n\)th term, so put the known values into \(a_{n} = a_{1} + (n-1)d\) and solve for \(n\).

Step 2: Solve for \(n\)
\[56 = (n-1) \times 7\]
\[n - 1 = 8\]
\[n = 9\]
Why: subtract 3 from both sides, then divide by 7. \(n\) must be a natural number, and 9 is.

blocks.title: Example 5
blocks.problem: If \(a_{n-2} = 3n - 11\), find the \(n\)th term of the sequence.
steps:
Given: \(a_{n-2} = 3n - 11\).
To find: \(a_{n}\).
Method: the rule gives the term in position \(n - 2\). To get position \(n\) we replace \(n\) by \(n + 2\) everywhere, because \((n + 2) - 2 = n\).

Step 1: Replace \(n\) by \(n + 2\)
\[a_{n+2-2} = 3(n+2) - 11\]
Why: the rule holds for every position, so it holds when \(n\) is replaced by \(n + 2\).

Step 2: Simplify
\[a_{n} = 3n + 6 - 11\]
\[a_{n} = 3n - 5\]
Why: \(n + 2 - 2 = n\) in the subscript, and \(3(n + 2) = 3n + 6\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Three terms in A.P.: \(a - d, a, a + d\); four terms: \(a - 3d, a - d, a + d, a + 3d\) (common difference \(2d\)); last four: \(\ell - 3d, \ell - 2d, \ell - d, \ell\).
2. Adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing every term by the same non-zero number keeps an A.P. an A.P.
3. Term-by-term sum or difference of two A.P.s is an A.P.
4. Two given terms give two equations in \(a_{1}\) and \(d\).
5. The number of terms is found from \(a_{n} = a_{1} + (n-1)d\) with \(a_{n}\) the last term.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
1. Taking \(d\) as the common difference of \(a - 3d, a - d, a + d, a + 3d\): it is \(2d\).
2. Sign slips: \((n - 1)(-3) = -3n + 3\), not \(-3n - 3\).
3. Forgetting that \(a_{1}\) is also a term when listing "the first four terms".
4. In Example 5, replacing \(n\) by \(n - 2\) instead of \(n + 2\).
